lesson.title: Locked In: Introducing Tuples
lesson.summary: A tuple is an ordered sequence of values, written with parentheses instead of square brackets, that behaves like a list except it cannot be changed once created, a restriction that turns out to be genuinely useful.
lesson.body:
You have already learned about Python's basic data types, and about lists as one way of grouping multiple values together. A tuple is another such grouping, and syntactically it looks almost identical to a list, using parentheses instead of square brackets: point = (3, 4). You can index into a tuple and iterate over it exactly as you would a list.

```python
point = (3, 4)
print(point[0])
print(point[1])

x, y = point
print(x, y)
```

This prints 3, then 4, then 3 4. That last pattern, x, y = point, is called tuple unpacking, and it is one of the most convenient features of tuples: it lets you pull a tuple's elements straight into separate named variables in a single line, which is exactly how many built-in functions and libraries hand back multiple related values at once, such as a coordinate pair or a min-and-max result.

The defining feature of a tuple, the one the name of this concept is built around, is that it is immutable: once created, its contents cannot be changed, added to, or removed from.

```python
point[0] = 5
```

This raises a TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment. Where a list happily accepts append, pop, and item assignment, a tuple refuses all of them outright. This is not a missing feature, it is the entire point. Immutability is a guarantee: once you hand a tuple to another part of your program, you know its contents cannot be silently altered behind your back, which makes tuples a natural fit for values that represent a fixed, small package of data, like a single x y coordinate or a red green blue color triple, that should never accidentally be modified. Immutability also has a second, more technical payoff: because a tuple cannot change, Python can use it as a dictionary key or store it inside a set, something a list, being mutable, is never allowed to do.

```python
locations = {(0, 0): 'origin', (1, 1): 'diagonal'}
print(locations[(0, 0)])
```

This prints origin. One syntax quirk is worth flagging explicitly, because it catches almost everyone at least once: parentheses alone do not make a tuple, the comma does. single = (5,) is a one-element tuple, but not_a_tuple = (5) is just the integer 5 with redundant parentheses around it, since Python treats a lone value in parentheses as a grouping, not a tuple. Checking type(single) confirms <class 'tuple'>, while type(not_a_tuple) confirms <class 'int'>. Finally, you can always build a tuple out of an existing list, or any iterable, with the tuple() constructor, as in tuple([1, 2, 3]), which returns (1, 2, 3); the reverse, list((1, 2, 3)), works the same way to turn a tuple back into a mutable list whenever you need one.
